name: rsync
summary: A file synchronization and copy tool that builds a file list, uses quick checks and block signatures to select changes, and transfers data over a remote shell or rsync daemon protocol.

features.name: File-list and quick-check planning
features.description: The generator side scans source paths into a sorted file list and applies a quick-check heuristic using metadata such as size and modification time, with an optional whole-file checksum check before selecting updates.
benefits: Avoids reading and transferring unchanged file contents in common cases
Makes the synchronization set explicit before transfer
costs: Metadata heuristics can miss changes when timestamps or sizes are not reliable
Large trees still incur scanning and file-list memory costs

features.name: Block-signature delta transfer
features.description: For selected regular files, rsync generates block signatures and the receiver tokenizes matching blocks or literal data so the sender transmits a reconstructed delta rather than necessarily sending the whole file.
benefits: Reduces network data for files with localized changes
Separates basis-file matching from final file reconstruction
costs: Signature generation and matching consume CPU and memory
Block boundaries and incompatible peers can reduce delta efficiency

features.name: Remote-shell and daemon transport boundary
features.description: rsync communicates either by starting a remote rsync process through a remote shell such as ssh or by connecting to an rsync daemon and selecting a configured module. These modes share file-transfer logic but have different admission and authentication boundaries.
benefits: Supports shell-mediated transfers without a persistent daemon
Supports controlled module exposure through a dedicated daemon
costs: Transport mode changes authentication, encryption, and path authorization assumptions
Both peers need compatible rsync behavior for negotiated protocol features

features.name: Metadata and destination update policy
features.description: The command and receiver paths support policies for permissions, times, ownership, links, backups, partial files, in-place writes, delayed updates, and deletion of destination entries. These policies are explicit options rather than an intrinsic guarantee of every run.
benefits: Lets operators choose preservation and failure-recovery semantics
Supports mirror, backup, and incremental-update workflows
costs: Option combinations create substantial filesystem semantics and security surface
In-place, deletion, and link handling can make partial failure consequential

mathematical_views.question: Which source and destination paths are selected for update under metadata, filter, and deletion policies?
assumptions: Source and destination trees are finite snapshots
Selection depends on quick checks, filters, and requested attributes
The relation does not claim that selected files are successfully transferred

mathematical_views.question: How are destination blocks and sender literals combined into the next file image?
assumptions: The receiver can expose a basis file to signature generation
Matching tokens identify reusable blocks while literals carry changed data
The view abstracts checksum algorithm negotiation and stream framing

mathematical_views.question: How does an rsync invocation enter local, remote-shell, or daemon/module transfer setup?
assumptions: Path syntax and options select a transport mode
The peer protocol and file-transfer state are downstream states
The model abstracts the remote shell implementation and socket details

costs: Metadata assumptions and file-list scans affect correctness and memory

benefits: Less network transfer for localized changes
costs: Matching consumes computation and does not always beat whole-file transfer

benefits: Flexible shell and daemon deployment modes
costs: Security and authorization properties differ by mode
Option interactions expand filesystem failure modes
